newsitem.title: USA: 57 U.S. senators back anti-land mine bill.
newsitem.headline: 57 U.S. senators back anti-land mine bill.

text.p: More than half of the members of the Senate Thursday announced a major push for legislation aimed at wiping out land mines.
The initiative was led by Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat who has campaigned against land mines for years, and Chuck Hagel, a Nebraska Republican who was wounded in Vietnam by a land mine.
Fifty-seven senators signed the initiative, including all but one of the Senate's nine Vietnam War veterans.

The bill would bar any U.S. agency from deploying or arming any new anti-personnel land mines after Jan. 1, 2000, except on the Korean Peninsula where it left discretion to the president for their use in case of a war or emergency.

Lawmakers also released a letter to President Clinton signed by more than 160 House members urging the United States to support an international treaty to ban land mines that Canada is promoting as a swifter solution than an alternative U.N.-related initiative being negotiated in Geneva.
There are an estimated 100 million land mines on the ground in 68 countries that hurt or kill 500 people every week, most of them civilians, Leahy said.
Each mine costs $3 to make -- and $300 to clear, he said.

"The damage done by these hidden killers long after the guns fall silent and the armies have gone home far outweigh whatever small benefits they add to our enormous and unsurpassed military arsenal," Leahy said.

"We are dealing with a different world than when we fought in World Wars, Korea and Vietnam," Hagel said. "Our recent military actions have been actions where we've been in and out relatively quickly. I am concerned with the effects of laying down mines and then leaving them behind when our troops leave."
